claims.text: Ingwë is described as being tall and beautiful, and his hair as golden and curly. He is also said to have been "more given to thought than arts".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, pp. 127-128; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: IV. Hair", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 186
claims.section: section == Characteristics ==

claims.text:
The name Ingwë is in Quenya. It means "chief", being derived from the root ING ("highest", "top"), to which is attached the suffix -wë ("person").
The Vanyar called themselves the Ingwer, the chieftains, on account of being considered the leaders and principal kindred of the Eldar, and their king's proper title was Ingwë Ingweron: ‘chief of the chieftains’.
In the earlier Etymologies, Ingwë is said to be a compound of ing ("first") + the ending -we ("man").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of Finwë's descendants", p. 340; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", entries"ING", "WEG"
claims.section: section == Etymology ==

claims.text: Ingwë was one of the Minyar born at Cuiviénen. He was the eldest son of Ilion, and a descendant of Imin and Iminyë, from eldest son to eldest son. He was beloved by his people, and at some point before the Great Journey he wed Ilwen and had several children at Cuiviénen by the time Oromë found the Quendi.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, pp. 127-128
claims.section: section == History ==

claims.text: When Oromë invited them to Aman, Ingwë, along with Finwë and Elwë, were the most eager to visit, and so followed him as ambassadors and travelled to the Blessed Realm. Once there, Ingwë desired to "dwell in the presence of Varda", and was reluctant to return to Middle-earth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XIII. Key Dates", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, pp. 96-98
claims.section: section == History ==

claims.text: When they returned, they held a great debate, and told their peoples about its beauty and bliss and became their leaders during the Great March. Ingwë was the leader of the Vanyar, the foremost of the clans to follow Oromë, who were the most eager to reach the West, which they did quickly.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Coming of the Elves and the Captivity of Melkor"
claims.section: section == History ==

claims.text: After the Great Journey, Ingwë never returned or set eyes upon Middle-earth again.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Coming of the Elves and the Captivity of Melkor"
claims.section: section == History ==

claims.text: He lived in Tirion for a while, where he also built the great, white tower at the topmost part of the city, called Mindon Eldaliéva or the Tower of Ingwë. It was never used, except by those who tended to the lamp at its summit.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, V. The Lhammas", p. 173
claims.section: section == History ==

claims.text: There he begot many children, as noted by Finwë when Finwë complained to the Valar about his widowhood.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: The Earliest Version of the Story of Finwë and Míriel", p. 206
claims.section: section == History ==

claims.text: At some point, however, he went to live on Taniquetil at the feet of Manwë.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Eldamar and the Princes of the Eldalië"
claims.section: section == History ==

claims.text: Indis, the second wife of Finwë, was of his close kin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Fëanor and the Unchaining of Melkor"
claims.section: section == History ==

claims.text:
The Gnomish cognate of Inwë is Inwithiel, changed from Gim Githil.
His proper (Gnomish) name, according to the Gnomish Lexicon was Inweg or Im, with Githil being the Gnomish cognate of Isil, another one of his names. Githiel was the poetic form of Githil.
The original Gnomish form of his name was Ginweg, later changed to Gim or Githil.
He was also called Tur yan Eldaron, meaning "King of the Elves" in Qenya, with Tur nan Églathon being its Gnomish equivalent.
In the Sketch of the Mythology, from c. 1926, the name Ing is described as being the Gnomish form of Ingwë, as opposed to the earlier conception of Ing being a rejected Qenya form of Inwë.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "I. The Cottage of Lost Play", p. 16; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "I. The Cottage of Lost Play", Changes made to names in The Cottage of Lost Play, p. 22; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, Appendix: Names in the Lost Tales - Part I, p. 256; J.R.R. Tolkien, "I-Lam na-Ngoldathon: The Grammar and Lexicon of the Gnomish Tongue", in Parma Eldalamberon XI (edited by Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), p. 39; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Qenyaqetsa: The Qenya Phonology and Lexicon", in Parma Eldalamberon XII (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), p. xx; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Sí Qente Feanor and Other Elvish Writings", in Parma Eldalamberon XV (edited by Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, Patrick H. Wynne, and Bill Welden), "Names and Required Alterations", Appendix, Text VIII, p. 16; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "II. The Earliest 'Silmarillion': Commentary on the Sketch of the Mythology", p. 44
claims.section: section == Other names ==

claims.text: In the early version of the legendarium, according to The Book of Lost Tales, the character that would later become known as Ingwë was called Inwë.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "I. The Cottage of Lost Play": "Notes and Commentary", p. 26
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: The name Inwë is in Qenya. In the Qenya Lexicon, it is said to be derived from the root INI ("small"), but the earlier, original gloss of the root was "fairy".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, Appendix: Names in the Lost Tales - Part I, p. 256; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Qenyaqetsa: The Qenya Phonology and Lexicon", in Parma Eldalamberon XII (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), pp. 42-3
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium > Early etymology

claims.text: In later outlines of the Book of Lost Tales, in which Tol Eressëa ceased to be identified with England, the island of Luthany appears as a precursor to England, from which the Elves of the Great Lands sail to Tol Eressëa, now a separate island.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "VI. The History of Eriol or Ælfwine and the End of the Tales", pp. 300-1
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium > Ingwë of Luthany

claims.text: In that conception of the legendarium, there appears a character called Ing or Ingwë, a Mannish King of Luthany who helps and welcomes the Elves to his land, after their war with Melko and, afterwards, with unfriendly Men in the Great Lands.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "VI. The History of Eriol or Ælfwine and the End of the Tales", outline 18, pp. 302-3
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium > Ingwë of Luthany

claims.text: However, he is not to be identified with the character of Inwë, or that of Ingwë in the later legendarium, even though Christopher Tolkien feels there has to be some connection between the two characters.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "VI. The History of Eriol or Ælfwine and the End of the Tales", outline 21, pp. 304-5
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium > Ingwë of Luthany

claims.text: Inwë might have spoken Inwelin, a dialect of Telellin spoken by the royal clan of Inwir.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Qenyaqetsa: The Qenya Phonology and Lexicon", in Parma Eldalamberon XII (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), p. 2
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: Inwë was one of the three Elves (the other two being Finwë and Tinwë) that volunteered to go with Nornorë, the messenger of the Valar, to Valinor, after their discovery at Koivië-néni - for Manwë wished to learn about their "coming" and their "desires".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "V. The Coming of the Elves and the Making of Kôr", p. 115
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: When Inwë arrived to Valinor, he was filled with wonder and longing for the light of Laurelin, one of the Two Trees, and his words moved Yavanna and Vána so that they convinced most of the other Valar to summon the Elves to Valinor to live amongst them. So Inwë and the other ambassadors were sent back to Koivië-néni, and managed to convince most of the Elves to come live with the Valar.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "V. The Coming of the Elves and the Making of Kôr", p. 116-8
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: Thereafter, Inwë became the leader of the Teleri, the first clan of the Elves, and led them to Valinor. He was also regarded as the eldest and greatest of all the Elves, and afterwards was considered the King of all the Eldar, and his home was at the highest point in Kôr, a great elven city in Valinor, which had a silver tower "shooting skyward like a needle". The Valar also gave Inwë a seedling of one of the Two Trees, which "blossomed eternally without abating" in his court.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "V. The Coming of the Elves and the Making of Kôr", p. 129; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "V. The Coming of the Elves and the Making of Kôr", p. 116; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "I. The Cottage of Lost Play", p. 16; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "V. The Coming of the Elves and the Making of Kôr", p. 122; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "V. The Coming of the Elves and the Making of Kôr", p. 123
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: And even though the Elves were victorious, and Melko defeated and bound by Tulkas, Inwë was, however, killed during the war.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "V. The Coming of the Elves and the Making of Kôr", p. 129
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: After the war, with the Elves being forbidden to return to Valinor, Ingil his son led them from the Great Lands to Tol Eressëa, the Lonely Isle, where he became their leader.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "VI. The History of Eriol or Ælfwine and the End of the Tales", outline 3, p. 280; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "I. The Cottage of Lost Play", p. 16
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: His kin and descendants were called the Inwir, one of whom was Meril-i-Turinqi his great-granddaughter, the Lady of Tol Eressëa at the time of the arrival of Eriol the Mariner, in c. 5th century AD.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "V. The Coming of the Elves and the Making of Kôr", p. 129; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "I. The Cottage of Lost Play": "Notes and Commentary", p. 26
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: In one outline, the island of Tol Eressëa was also called Inwinórë after Inwë, but that was later changed to Ingilnórë, in honour of his son Ingil instead.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Qenyaqetsa: The Qenya Phonology and Lexicon", in Parma Eldalamberon XII (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), p. xiii
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Early legendarium

claims.text: In the Lhammas, a text from the 1930s, Ingwë is mentioned as one of the original, and the eldest, of the Elves to be awakened at Cuiviénen, and who led his people, chief of whom were known as the Ingwelindar or Ingwi, to Aman.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, V. The Lhammas", p. 171
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Later legendarium > Quenta Noldorinwa and the Lhammas

claims.text: In the Quenta Noldorinwa from c. 1930, he was still supposed to be one of the leaders of the Eldar in the War of Wrath (unlike in the later versions, where it was his son Ingwion who led them), and he was still supposed to die in that war, as in the early legendarium in the Book of Lost Tales.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "III. The Quenta: Commentary on the Quenta, [Section] 2", p. 168
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Later legendarium > Quenta Noldorinwa and the Lhammas

claims.text: Finally, Imin agreed to a vote, and about two thirds of the Elves gathered at the time agreed to go to Aman.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XIII. Key Dates", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, pp. 96-98
